\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{گاؤں} (gāoṅ)}{گاؤں (gāoṅ)}]{\ur{گاؤں} (gāoṅ) — a village}

\label{lesson:UR-C293-gaon}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for destruction, then the Urdu for an effect.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{گاؤں}}
\textbf{\ur{گاؤں}} — \emph{gāoṅ} — \textquotedblleft{}a village\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ur{ہمارا} \ur{گاؤں} \ur{دریا} \ur{کے} \ur{کنارے} \ur{ہے۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{hamārā gāoṅ daryā ke kināre hai.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Our village is on the bank of the river.
\end{quote}

Masculine.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{گاؤں}} (\emph{gāoṅ}) is inherited from Sanskrit \emph{grāma}, \textquotedblleft{}a village\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 4368), where CDIAL lists the Hindi cousin \emph{gā̃u}. Urdu writes it with \textbf{\ur{ؤ}} and the nasal \textbf{\ur{ں}}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{gāoṅ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{gāoṅ}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{hamārā gāoṅ daryā ke kināre hai.} — Our village is on the bank of the river.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Urdu for destruction, then the Urdu for an effect, then say \emph{gāoṅ} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ur{گاؤں} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}A village\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{بہنا} (bahnā)}{بہنا (bahnā)}]{\ur{بہنا} (bahnā) — to flow; to be swept away}

\label{lesson:UR-C293-bahna}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for an effect, then the Urdu for a village.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{بہنا}}
\textbf{\ur{بہنا}} — \emph{bahnā} — \textquotedblleft{}to flow; to be swept away\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ur{پانی} \ur{گلیوں} \ur{میں} \ur{بہہ} \ur{رہا} \ur{تھا۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{pānī galiyoṅ meṅ bah rahā thā.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Water was flowing through the lanes.
\end{quote}

Past (it …): \ur{وہ} \ur{پل} \ur{بہہ} \ur{گیا}, \emph{voh pul bah gayā}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{بہنا}} (\emph{bahnā}) is inherited: CDIAL lists the Hindi cousin \emph{bahnā}, \textquotedblleft{}flows, blows\textquotedblright{}, under Sanskrit \emph{váhati} (CDIAL 11453). Its stem is written \textbf{\ur{بہہ}}: \textbf{\ur{بہہ} \ur{گیا}}, was swept away.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bahnā}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{pānī galiyoṅ meṅ bah rahā thā.} — Water was flowing through the lanes.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Urdu for an effect, then the Urdu for a village, then say \emph{bahnā} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{ڈوبنا} (ḍūbnā)}{ڈوبنا (ḍūbnā)}]{\ur{ڈوبنا} (ḍūbnā) — to sink; to drown}

\label{lesson:UR-C293-dubna}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for a village, then the Urdu for to flow.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{ڈوبنا}}
\textbf{\ur{ڈوبنا}} — \emph{ḍūbnā} — \textquotedblleft{}to sink; to drown\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ur{تمام} \ur{گاؤں} \ur{پانی} \ur{میں} \ur{ڈوب} \ur{گیا۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{tamām gāoṅ pānī meṅ ḍūb gayā.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The whole village went under water.
\end{quote}

Past (it …): \ur{وہ} \ur{کشتی} \ur{ڈوب} \ur{گئی}, \emph{voh kashtī ḍūb gaī}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{ڈوبنا}} (\emph{ḍūbnā}) is inherited: CDIAL lists the Hindi cousin \emph{ḍūbnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to sink\textquotedblright{}, under \emph{*ḍubb}, a form it reconstructs (CDIAL 5561). A person who \textbf{\ur{ڈوب} \ur{گیا}} drowned.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{بھنور} (bhanvar)}{بھنور (bhanvar)}]{\ur{بھنور} (bhanvar) — a whirlpool}

\label{lesson:UR-C293-bhanvar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for to sink, then the Urdu for a wave.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{بھنور}}
\textbf{\ur{بھنور}} — \emph{bhanvar} — \textquotedblleft{}a whirlpool\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ur{دریا} \ur{میں} \ur{ایک} \ur{بھنور} \ur{تھا۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{daryā meṅ ek bhanvar thā.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
There was a whirlpool in the river.
\end{quote}

Masculine.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{بھنور}} (\emph{bhanvar}) is inherited: CDIAL lists the Hindi cousin \emph{bhãwar}, \textquotedblleft{}a whirlpool\textquotedblright{}, under Sanskrit \emph{bhramara} (CDIAL 9650), a word for what turns round and round.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
